4.0.0.en: "His hands were feeble": he felt weak and lost control of matters.

4.0.1.en: Abner was the real manager in the kingdom of Israel, not Ishbosheth, who was only a nominal king, and Abner was a politician and a strong military commander. When the news of his death reached the kingdom of Israel, Ishbosheth felt that the support of the kingdom was gone and sensed his weakness without him, and the people of the tribes subject to him were afraid because they had become without a commander to protect them and were exposed to punishment from David for their rebellion against him and their following of Ishbosheth. But David was a gentle and forgiving man, so he did no evil and did not punish the tribes. We note that the name of Ishbosheth is not mentioned in this verse, but the inspired text says "Saul's son," in contempt of him and because he had lost his strength, that is, Abner.

4.1.0.en: "Captains of bands": heads of military companies.

4.1.1.en: Beeroth: a city in the tribe of Benjamin, 15 km north of Jerusalem. It was originally one of the cities of the Gibeonites, and the tribe of Benjamin took it.

4.1.2.en: Among the men of war belonging to Ishbosheth there were two heads of military companies named "Baanah" and "Rechab," the two sons of a man named Rimmon, from the town of Beeroth, which belonged to the tribe of Benjamin.

4.2.0.en: The Beerothites are the inhabitants of the town of Beeroth, and they were a mixture of Gibeonites and Benjamites. When Saul was angry with the Gibeonites (ch. 21:1), the people of Beeroth fled to a town called "Gittaim," fleeing from Saul's persecution of them. They remained there until the time of the writing of this book.

4.3.1.en: Jonathan the son of Saul had a son named "Mephibosheth," who was five years old when Saul and Jonathan were killed in their last battle against the Philistines in Jezreel. The child's nurse was afraid that the Philistines would harm him, so she picked him up to flee with him to any safe place, but as she ran the child fell from her to the ground and his feet were injured, and he became lame to the end of his life.

4.3.2.en: Mephibosheth is mentioned here because he and Ishbosheth were the ones left of the descendants of Saul, and Mephibosheth was not fit to be king because of the weakness of his feet, and also because this is a preparation for the good that David would do to him afterwards (ch. 9:1-9). That is, with the killing of Ishbosheth there is no one left for Saul to reign on his throne.

4.4.0.en: Baanah and Rechab sensed Ishbosheth's weakness after the death of Abner, so they thought of a plot to kill him and bring this news to David, so as to receive a great reward from him, such as becoming commanders in his armies. They forgot that David was a loving and forgiving man who hated evil, and that he had killed the one who brought him news of the death of Saul and Jonathan (ch. 1:16). So they planned to kill their king Ishbosheth, and for this to be done at midday when he was asleep and at a time when no one expects harm to befall the king because it is daytime.

4.5.0.en: "The plain": the plain beside the Jordan.

4.5.1.en: These two brothers were assigned to grind wheat and distribute it to the soldiers, so their entering the house was a customary matter that aroused no suspicion. When they reached where the king was lying, they found him deep in sleep, so they struck him in the belly and he died at once. Then they cut off his head and left from there in flight, with no one aware of them, and walked the rest of the day and all night through the plain beside the Jordan, heading for Hebron.

4.6.0.en: The two brothers came to David in Hebron with the severed head, and presented it to him, saying that it was the head of Ishbosheth the son of Saul, his enemy who had pursued him all the days, trying to seize him and kill him, and that God had avenged him on Saul and his descendants, for He permitted them to kill his son who was competing with him for the kingship over the people of Israel. But God was not pleased with the treachery and evil they did to their king, and He used their evil to accomplish His will in David's reigning, and they should not have wronged their king, for God has different ways of carrying out His will.

4.6.1.en: Do not do evil to please people or in seeking your own interest, and do not forget that God watches all the deeds of human beings and repays them for them. Always remember that God sees you, so that you do what pleases Him.

4.7.s.en: (2) David kills the murderers of Ishbosheth

4.7.0.en: David's reaction to this event was contrary to what the two murderers "Baanah and Rechab" expected, for David declared that the living God was the One who had redeemed him out of all adversity, and not the arm of a human being, as these two murderers thought that by killing Ishbosheth they were establishing the kingdom for David.

4.8.0.en: "Gave him a reward for his tidings": I killed him in return for these tidings, for which he thought he would be rewarded well. David recalled the story of the Amalekite man who thought that by bringing him the news of the death of Saul he was coming to David with good news that would please him greatly, and David commanded that he be killed in "Ziklag" (ch. 1:15, 16), so his killing was the recompense he deserved for what he thought was pleasing good news, while its effect on David was completely the opposite.

4.9.0.en: "Take you away from the earth": kill you.

4.9.1.en: The deed of the Amalekite man was less criminal, for Saul had been severely wounded and was about to fall into the hands of the Philistines, and yet David considered him condemned and deserving of death. How much more, then, what these two persons committed of conspiracy and treachery by their sinful assault on Ishbosheth, whom David in his love described as a righteous man, for they stabbed him while he slept in his bed. David sentenced them to death, as they had done to the life of an innocent person, for it would not have been just for their recompense to be less than the Amalekite's.

4.9.2.en: David enjoyed the simple outlook with which he saw the virtues of his enemies, so he praised Saul in his lament and here describes Ishbosheth as a righteous man. May you see the virtues of the one who wrongs you so that you love him and make excuses for him in his mistakes, and so live by the commandment of Christ, that is, love of enemies.

4.10.0.en: David commanded his soldiers and they killed the two men, because he wanted not to defile his kingdom with acts of treachery, and to declare that his reigning is not accomplished by betrayal and treachery but by the power of God. So they cut off their hands, which had killed an innocent person, and cut off their feet, which had entered the chamber of the innocent man to carry out their crime, and hanged their bodies in a place frequented by many people, the pool of Hebron, so that everyone would see the consequence of transgression and betrayal, and as proof of David's love for Saul and his descendants and honor to Ishbosheth because he was a king and the son of a king. David decided to bury his head in the tomb in which Abner had been buried before in Hebron, the capital of David's kingdom at that time.

4.10.1.en: Ishbosheth and Abner differed and quarreled, and the days passed and both were buried in one tomb in Hebron. May we remember death so that we live in peace with those around us and forgive whoever wrongs us, because death will bring us together and we take nothing from this world.

4.10.2.en: David as king over all Israel and his victories over the Jebusites and the Philistines

5.0.s.en: (1) David as king over all Israel

5.0.0.en: "We are thy bone and thy flesh": we are your relatives, for he is of the tribe of Judah and they are the descendants of the brothers of Judah.

5.0.1.en: After the events mentioned in the two preceding chapters of the killing of Abner, the commander of Ishbosheth's army, and then the killing of Ishbosheth himself, none of Saul's descendants remained alive except Mephibosheth his grandson, who was lame in his feet and therefore unfit to take the kingship, besides Abner's effort to hand the kingdom over to David. So the elders of Israel from the eleven tribes came to David in Hebron, declaring their kinship to him and therefore their submission and their acceptance of his being king over them.

5.1.0.en: "Leddest out and broughtest in Israel": you led the armies outside and inside Israel.

5.1.1.en: They acknowledged before him that he had been leading their armies successfully during the reign of Saul, whether outside the country or inside it, and they also acknowledged what they had heard from Samuel, that the Lord would take the kingdom from Saul and give it to another better than he (1 Sam 15:28), and that all the events confirm that he is the one chosen by the Lord to reign over His people and shepherd them.

5.2.0.en: The heads and leaders of the people came to Hebron to pledge allegiance to David, and he made a covenant with them before the Lord that he would govern his people according to the divine Law and be faithful in shepherding them, and in return the people pledged to obey him and be faithful to him. All the tribes anointed him to be king over Israel.

5.2.1.en: This is the third anointing of David. The first was secretly in his father's house in the lifetime of Saul (1 Sam 16:13), and the second was the anointing by the men of Judah in Hebron (ch. 2:4) after the death of Saul to be king over them.

5.2.2.en: God prepared David to be king by the following:

5.2.3.en: 1- He taught him patience and endurance when he endured Saul's wrongs and his pursuit of him.

5.2.4.en: 2- He taught him humility when he humbled himself before Saul, the king rejected by God, and did not seek the kingship for himself.

5.2.5.en: 3- He taught him detachment when he lived driven out in the mountains and valleys and dwelling among the enemies during Saul's pursuit.

5.2.6.en: 4- He experienced faith and reliance on God, who rescued him from the hand of Saul and from the hand of the Philistines and all who were hostile to him, until in the end He established him king over all Israel.

5.2.7.en: 5- He taught him not to avenge himself, in his forbearance with Saul, who tried to kill him, and his endurance of Abner and Ishbosheth.

5.3.0.en: David's age when he took the kingship was thirty years, and he remained king for forty years, reigning over Israel until he died at the age of seventy. The age of thirty is the age of maturity among the Jews, at which a man's opinion is taken into account, and it is the same age at which Joseph became ruler of Egypt and at which Christ began His ministry.

5.4.0.en: The exact total length of his reign is forty years and six months, divided into two periods. The first is the period of his reign over the tribe of Judah only, and the seat of his rule during it was in Hebron, and its length was seven years and six months, beginning from the death of Saul until the death of Ishbosheth the son of Saul. The second period, thirty years, was when he reigned over all the tribes of Israel, and the seat of his rule in it was the city of Jerusalem.

5.4.1.en: When God wishes and the time is fulfilled, He restores your rights to you and makes everyone submit to you. David waited long years after being anointed king by the hand of Samuel until his reign over all the people was completed. So be patient and continue in your prayers until you receive your rights, and do not forget that your first and most important right is the Kingdom of Heaven, so care for repentance and the growth of your relationship with God before any material thing, and God will remove your sins from you however long the time, and will make your faith grow so that you enjoy fellowship with Him.

5.5.0.en: The Jebusites: a tribe of the Canaanites who dwelt in Jebus, which is Jerusalem.

5.5.1.en: "Except thou take away the blind and the lame": the blind and the lame among the Jebusites are able to repel you, for they are stronger than the men of your army. In this there is a challenge and mockery of David and his army.

5.5.2.en: Jerusalem: its name was formerly Salem or Shalem, that is, king of peace, and from it came Melchizedek, priest of the Most High God (Gen 14:18). It lies on five mountains, among them Mount Zion and Mount Moriah, and rises about 700 meters above sea level and lies about 22 km west of the Dead Sea. It lies north of the tribe of Judah and near the tribe of Benjamin. It was anciently called Jebus after the Jebusites, its inhabitants, and although Joshua killed its king among the five kings (Josh 10:13-26), the Jebusites returned and took possession of it, and the tribe of Judah burned most of it, yet the Jebusites did not leave it but continued to dwell in the high, fortified places in it, while the Benjamites dwelt in the lower parts (Josh 15:36). After the eleven tribes joined the tribe of David in a united kingdom that David ruled, David decided to move the capital of his kingdom from Hebron to Jerusalem, where the Jebusites were living, so he had to fight them in order to take their city Jerusalem, which they called Jebus. The Jebusites were fortified in their land and fully confident of its impregnability, that no one could invade it, so they mocked David when they heard his decision to fight them, saying their phrase famous at that time, which means that the blind and the lame in their city were stronger and mightier than the men of his army and than he himself. The meaning of their saying was that these blind and lame would be the ones to defend the city and were enough to prevent him from entering it, so they showed him his weakness so that he would draw back from fighting them. David chose Jerusalem to be the capital of his kingdom for the following reasons:

5.5.3.en: 1- Its central location among the tribes.

5.5.4.en: 2- Its fortified location, because it is built on mountains, so it is hard to fight against.

5.5.5.en: 3- The Jebusites lived in it, so it did not belong to any of the tribes, and thus he did not take a city from any tribe, and so does not become subordinate to any tribe.

5.5.6.en: 4- It was adjacent to the tribe of Benjamin and some Benjamites lived in it, and by this he won the affection of this tribe, from which Saul came, so that peace would be established in his kingdom. It also falls within the tribe of Judah, so by this he pleased the tribe of Judah as well, which is his own.

5.6.0.en: David succeeded in taking the city despite the claims of its inhabitants the Jebusites, and David called the city "the city of David."

5.6.1.en: The following verses relate the details of David's taking it. The stronghold of Zion mentioned lies in the south-east of Jerusalem; it is a high mountain in which the Jebusites fortified themselves, and David took it, then built a temple for the Lord on Mount Moriah, and the name Zion widened to express all of Jerusalem.

5.7.0.en: David wanted to kindle the enthusiasm of his men, so he set a reward for whoever crossed through the water channel into the land of the Philistines, and reached the position of the Jebusite guards of the walls and fought them and defeated them. The guards were neither blind nor lame, but they said that as a challenge and mockery of David. The setting of a reward is not mentioned in this verse, but it is mentioned in (1 Chr 11:6), namely that whoever does that will be chief and commander.

5.7.1.en: David's saying that the blind and the lame are hated of his soul means the Jebusites in general. David hated them for their idolatry and for the challenge and contempt they showed toward his person and toward the people of the Lord, and David's saying about the lame and the blind became a proverb that people repeated. They say, "No blind or lame shall enter the house of the Lord," that is, there is no longer a Jebusite to enter the house of the Lord, or it is forbidden for any pagan like the Jebusites to enter the house of the Lord. The word Jebusite means trodden under foot, so it is a type of Satan, whom Christ trod down by His Cross, and Christ is the descendant of David and David is a type of Him, and Christ achieved this victory over Satan, as David triumphed over the Jebusites, in order to give this power of His to everyone who believes in Him, so that he treads down the power of Satan and drives him out of his life.

5.8.0.en: After David took the city he called it the city of David, and he built it up and built many houses in it extending from the wall of the city to its middle.

5.9.0.en: David's standing grew ever more brilliant and prosperous, and God was the secret of his strength, for He is the God of hosts, who sends His angels to help and support His children.

5.9.1.en: Do not be troubled by the threats of the wicked if they exalt themselves over you and mock you, for the Lord is with you, so no one can prevail against you. Be firm in your faith, holding fast to God's commandments, and you will succeed in the end like David.

5.10.s.en: (3) Hiram helps in building a house for David

5.10.0.en: Hiram king of Tyre: he reigned 34 years over the kingdom of Tyre, and he had friendly relations and friendship with both David and Solomon.

5.10.1.en: Hiram king of Tyre was a friend of David, so he sent him much timber with skilled carpenters and masons to help him in building a great palace for himself. Tyre was distinguished by the presence of cedar trees, strong in their wood, and by carpenters skilled in the craft of woodwork. Here the blessings of God to His striving children appear, for He supported David in driving the pagans out of Jebus, then rewarded him with Hiram's gifts.

5.11.0.en: David saw and became certain that the Lord was the One working to establish his kingdom and also the One working to magnify his kingdom, because of His love for His people and His desire to make them happy. Whoever pleases the Lord, He gives him favor in the eyes of those around him, so they are at peace with him and even try to win his affection.

5.11.1.en: It is beautiful of David to attribute the credit for all that he came to of greatness and exaltation to the Lord, who supported and strengthened him. Let us humble ourselves before the Lord so that we may have spiritual insight to discern that all the success that comes to us is not the fruit of our strength or human abilities but is a grace and gift from the Lord, and so we thank Him every day.

5.12.s.en: (4) The sons born to David in Jerusalem

5.12.0.en: David took wives and concubines, as was the custom of the kings of those times, in addition to his wives that he had when he was in Hebron, who are mentioned in (ch. 3:2-5). But sadly the great number of wives did not protect David from falling into his lust for Bathsheba and committing adultery with her. Rather, what protects is chastity and the fear of God, as Joseph did (Gen 39:11-15).

5.13.0.en: The first four are "Shammua," "Shobab," "Nathan" and "Solomon," who are the sons of Bathsheba the wife of Uriah the Hittite, and Shammua has another name by which he is mentioned in (1 Chr 3:5), which is "Shimea."

5.14.0.en: "Ibhar" is also mentioned in (1 Chr 3:6, 14:5), and "Elishua," whose name appears as "Elishama" in (1 Chr 3:6), and "Nepheg" (also spelled "Nefeg"), who is also mentioned in (1 Chr 3:7 and 14:6).

5.15.0.en: "Elishama" is also mentioned in (1 Chr 3:8), "Eliada" is also mentioned as "Eliada" in (1 Chr 3:8), and in (1 Chr 14:7) he is called "Beeliada."

5.15.1.en: "Eliphalet" or "Eliphelet" was born after the death of the son mentioned with the same name in (1 Chr 3:8 and 14:7). The First Book of Chronicles (chs. 3, 14) adds two other sons to the eleven sons mentioned here, namely Nogah and Eliphelet, and the inspired text did not mention them here because they died young.

5.15.2.en: If you have physical children, take care to bring them up in the fear of God, but the most important thing is that you acquire virtues, and love and serve those around you, and care for the salvation of their souls, for all these are your spiritual children who remain with you forever in the Kingdom of Heaven.

5.16.0.en: When David's kingdom began to grow and expand through the joining of all the tribes to him, the Philistines began to fear him, so they planned to fight him before the growth of his kingdom was complete and made preliminary reconnaissance movements. When the news of these movements reached David, he took refuge in a fortified place to arrange matters with his commanders.

5.17.0.en: The valley of Rephaim: a fertile valley between Bethlehem and Jerusalem. The Philistines spread their forces in the "valley of Rephaim."

5.18.0.en: As was David's custom before undertaking any move, he asked the Lord whether he should go up to confront the Philistines and whether He would give him victory over them, and the Lord answered him yes.

5.19.0.en: Baal-perazim: a high place north of the valley of Rephaim.

5.19.1.en: "The Lord hath broken forth upon mine enemies before me, as the breach of waters": the Lord burst upon the enemies as the rushing waters burst through everything that stands in their way.

5.19.2.en: David advanced to meet the Philistines, and the confrontation took place at a place later called "Baal-perazim," that is, the lord of breaking through, where David won a splendid victory, and as was his custom he ascribed the victory to the Lord who supported him, and His power advanced through the ranks, bursting upon the enemies, therefore the place was called "the lord of breaking through."

5.20.0.en: The Philistines had carried their idols in the midst of their armies, as was the custom of peoples anciently, thinking that these gods of theirs would help them achieve victory. When the Philistines were defeated and fled, they had no time to take their idols with them in their retreat, so they left them at the place of the battle, and David and his men destroyed them and burned them with fire so that they would not be a stumbling block to the people afterwards.

5.21.0.en: The Philistines did not surrender after their first defeat, but waged another war to take revenge on David and his kingdom, so they massed their armies in the same place, that is, in the valley of Rephaim.

5.22.0.en: Mulberry trees (baca trees): a kind of tree from which a sap comes out resembling tears.

5.22.1.en: The host of the Philistines: the camp of the Philistines, where they fortify themselves.

5.22.2.en: As was David's custom, he turned to prayer to the Lord, asking whether he should fight the Philistines. The Lord was not content with answering him with approval or refusal, but also directed him to the plan he should follow to gain the victory. He commanded him not to confront them from the front as the previous time, but to circle around them until he was behind them and to hide in an area thick with trees, and when he heard the sound of regular steps like the steps of a mighty army, as if coming from the tops of the trees, then he would know that the Lord was present with him and going before him to give him victory over the army of the enemies, and he should come out of his hiding place and fight them.

5.22.3.en: The Lord is present with His children at all times as long as they seek Him. When some trials or hard circumstances surround us, let us trust that God will stretch out a helping hand to us and bring us out of distress into a broad place. We only have to call upon Him, for He is near and answers those who call upon Him.

5.23.0.en: Geba: a city in Benjamin on the northern edge of the kingdom of Judah, that is, north-east of Jerusalem, and it was assigned for the dwelling of the priests (Josh 21:17). Gazer: a city in the land of the tribe of Judah lying on the border of the land of the Philistines, north-west of Jerusalem.

5.23.1.en: David carried out the plan the Lord had drawn for him with all precision, so the Philistines were defeated before him and fled, and David pursued them with his army from Geba until they reached Gazer, where the children of Israel stopped pursuing them. That is, the Philistines did not flee to their land, which lies west of Jerusalem, but fled to the north-east of Jerusalem, that is, the city of Geba, to fortify themselves there, and since they found no opportunity to fortify themselves, they turned back and headed west toward their land and went by the road of the Jewish city of Gazer, which lies on the border of the land of the Philistines. The bringing of the ark to the city of David: more details of the carrying and moving of the ark are found in (1 Chr 13, 15, 16)
